text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a power station with about 1,000 Wh of battery to cover most of a day. For a full 24 hours or more, plan on 1,400-2,000 Wh. The inverter should handle a startup surge of at least 1,300 W and output pure sine wave power.

**What to check**
- **Running watts:** a full-size fridge draws roughly 100-250 W while the compressor runs, so almost any 1,000 W-class station covers it ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
- **Startup surge:** the compressor spikes when it kicks on. Sources put it at about 900-1,200 W ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)), up to 1,300 W ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)), or even 2,400 W ([BlackBox](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). A station that can't cover the spike will trip even with a big battery.
- **Battery (Wh):** the compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time. One estimate for a typical fridge averages about 41 W, or roughly 990 Wh a day. Adding inverter losses and 20% headroom gives about 1,400 Wh per 24 hours ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- **Your own fridge:** the yellow EnergyGuide label lists kWh per year. Divide by 8.76 for average watts. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average about twice the ENERGY STAR figure, and a small apartment fridge about half.

**Estimated runtimes** (HomeGrid HQ, assuming 85% inverter efficiency and a 35% duty cycle):
- About 1,000 Wh: roughly 17 hours
- About 1,500 Wh: roughly 25 hours
- About 2,000 Wh: roughly 33 hours

([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). Keep the door shut. The USDA says food is unsafe after 4 hours above 40°F, so the goal is to keep the fridge cold.

**Options that fit**
- **BLUETTI AC180** (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W with 2,700 W peak, about $399-699): a good fit for most of a day. See [BlackBox's guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) for current pricing.
- **BLUETTI AC200L** (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous, 3,600 W surge): covers a full day and more, about 33 hours in HomeGrid's estimate. It lists at $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF, which Dealectric says it tested in BLUETTI's cart on 2026-10-21. Checkout has the final word on price. [Buy at BLUETTI](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) (affiliate link, so Dealectric earns a commission at no cost to you). Details are on the [product page](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l).
- **Anker SOLIX S2000** (2 kWh class, $699.99 after coupon): see [Anker's sizing guide](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator). It is a lower-priced 2 kWh option, but I don't have its specs beyond the capacity class.
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2** (1,070 Wh, about $449-799): similar to the AC180, at roughly 17 hours. See [BlackBox's guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage).

If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year, how long an outage you want to cover, and what else you'd plug in, I can narrow this down.
